lead: The experiments support explicit contributions, Rust-described API contracts with generated clients and explicit bounds, stable operation identities, and complete cached-scope refreshes. The audit exposed important restore and provenance assumptions.

choices.title: Explicit contributor rows
choices.text: Keep source, manual, known total-setting adjustments and unknown legacy adjustments distinct. Source corrections replace one contribution. Full command history was not required by the exercised behaviors.

choices.title: Generated types plus validators
choices.text: Rust/utoipa with openapi-typescript and Ajv standalone is the stronger of the two exercised pipelines. Enum closure, suppression, dates and numeric range still need explicit contract decisions.

choices.title: Stable operation IDs
choices.text: Deduplicate by client installation and immutable operation ID. Conditional versions still depend on a controlled restore that mints a new generation before serving. A plain file restore can reuse stale tokens.

choices.title: Complete scope refreshes
choices.text: Replace cached date ranges and preserve the separate outbox. Validators need temporal identity only when the representation depends on today. No initial change feed was required by the exercised scenarios.

product_choices: Define manual contribution set separately from aggregate replacement or a pinned override. Decide activity-day attribution and who may make restored source history authoritative. Passing traces cannot choose those meanings.
next: Specify contributor rows and a small versioned API, then build one manual observation, one versioned source-day replacement and one chart-independent series query through the real Rust HTTP adapter and generated client. Prove migration and device behavior before replacing current consumers.
limits: Synthetic observations, not production acceptance. Storage variants share a reducer; sync uses a simplified INTEGER table rather than the selected full codec. SQLite restore and cache-only HTTP were exercised. Real migration, concurrent writers, process kills, automatic restore detection, pending-write overlays and RN/Hermes remain unproved. No performance benefit was measured.
review: Reviewed by claude-opus-5-5. Exploratory evidence accepted. Parent added restore/ID-reuse counterexamples and corrected known-adjustment provenance; those narrow revisions were rerun, not independently re-audited.
api_summary: Both generated paths accepted all 64 exercised Rust-serialized outputs, but four full-i64 fixtures changed decimal spelling or value in the JavaScript round trip. Neither path exactly matched raw Rust parsing.
api_lessons: SafeNumber and OpaqueRevision constraints were handwritten Rust schema builders. The contract was not inferred automatically from every constructor.

Full-i64 JSON numbers lost digits in JavaScript. Safe-range numbers worked for the exercised ordinary values. Decide the supported product range before narrowing any legacy contract; opaque version tokens avoid arithmetic encoding.

Canonical decimal strings preserved full-i64 values, but generated regex validation did not enforce i64 arithmetic bounds. The matching BigInt refinement is handwritten and remains a second authority.

Unknown enum fields and suppressed goals behaved differently across Rust, emitted schema and decoders. Ajv followed the emitted schema more closely; it cannot repair a schema that does not describe Rust's behavior.
The comparison Zod generator is deprecated and its exported scalar roots lost constraints. This supports a toolchain candidate, not a claim that every Zod-based generator fails.
Dates, duplicate JSON keys, lexical integers and interval ordering need explicit boundary/domain rules. Generated types compile; that alone does not prove parser or product equivalence.
Choose unknown-field policy separately for requests and responses. Closed response schemas can break installed mobile clients when compatible fields are added.
